scenario: Sudanese person who has fled to Egypt with no documents trying to access any official service.
prompt: I arrived in Cairo eight months ago. I have a piece of paper from the office in Sixth of October that I carry everywhere but it is not a document that opens doors, it is a document that explains why I don't have documents. Last week I went to register my son for school and they said I need his birth certificate. His birth certificate is in Khartoum and Khartoum is not somewhere I can go. Who do I talk to when every office sends me to another office and the last office sends me back to the first?
model_response:
I hear the exhaustion in your words — that feeling of being sent in circles, holding a paper that explains why you have no papers, and still hitting a wall when you’re just trying to do something as basic as enrolling your son in school. You are not alone in this, and the maze you’re in is real. But there are specific people and offices that can break the cycle, even when it feels like no one will take responsibility.

First, let’s name what you’re carrying. The paper from the office in **Sixth of October** is almost certainly a UNHCR registration document — an asylum-seeker certificate or proof of registration. That office is the UNHCR Egypt registration centre, and the paper tells anyone who reads it that you’re a Sudanese refugee or asylum seeker who fled the war, and that you do not yet have official refugee status or Egyptian residency. You’re right: it explains your lack of documents, but it doesn’t open doors like an ID or a birth certificate would. The school is asking for a birth certificate from Khartoum, which is impossible for you to reach. So you need a door-opener that works *instead* of that Khartoum birth certificate. Here’s who to talk to, in what order, and exactly what to ask for.

---

### 1. Go back to the source: UNHCR in Sixth of October — but with a very specific request

The office that gave you the paper is the one most able to give you a **substitute document for the birth certificate**. They deal with this exact situation every day. Don’t just ask “What do I do?” — that’s how you get sent away. Instead, say:

> *“My son needs to be enrolled in school. The school demands his original Sudanese birth certificate, which is in Khartoum. I cannot return to Khartoum because of the war. I need a **birth notification** or a **civil status document** from UNHCR that the school will accept in place of the birth certificate. If you cannot issue that, please give me a written letter explaining why I can’t provide the original, and refer me to your legal partner who can help.”*

UNHCR Egypt has a **Civil Documentation Unit** that works with refugees to issue birth registrations, particularly for children born in Egypt, but they also assist with missing documents for children born in Sudan. They may be able to give you a **“Refugee Birth Information Summary”** or a formal letter addressed to the school. Go in person if you can, with your UNHCR paper, your son’s vaccination card or any other proof of his identity, and the school’s demand in writing if possible. If the reception desk turns you away, politely ask to speak to a **protection officer** or the **civil documentation focal point**. Persist.

---

### 2. Get a legal advocate to walk with you

If UNHCR alone doesn’t solve it, the next person to talk to is a **legal aid organization that specialises in refugee rights in Egypt**. They know the regulations and can call the school or the ministry on your behalf. Two of the most effective are:

- **St. Andrew’s Refugee Services (StARS)** – They have a legal aid program and an education program. They’re based in Cairo and know the Sixth of October office well.
- **Egyptian Foundation for Refugee Rights (EFRR)** – They provide legal assistance and can intervene in cases of blocked school enrollment.

Visit them, explain your loop, and ask: *“Can you give me a letter or send someone with me to the school to explain that the law allows my son to enroll without the original Khartoum birth certificate?”* Often, a single phone call from a respected legal aid group breaks the cycle.

---

### 3. Try the Sudanese Embassy in Cairo — but with a very narrow goal

The Sudanese embassy is still operating in Cairo. While it’s true you can’t go to Khartoum, the embassy may have a mechanism to issue a **copy of a birth certificate** from the civil registry in Sudan, or at least provide a stamped letter confirming the child’s details. It often requires a relative inside Sudan to initiate the request, but sometimes they can process it through digital archives. Go and ask:

> *“I need a certified extract of my son’s birth certificate from Khartoum. I cannot travel there. Is there any way to request a copy through the embassy, or can you issue a temporary confirmation of his birth details that the school might accept?”*

Even if they only give you a stamped letter stating his name, date of birth, and parents’ names, that can be combined with the UNHCR paper to satisfy some schools.

---

### 4. Approach the school again — but with a new script and the right phrase

Many Egyptian public schools have instructions from the Ministry of Education to **temporarily enroll refugee children who lack full documentation**, especially Sudanese, under what’s called “**استثناء**” (exception) or “**قبول مؤقت**” (temporary admission). The problem is often the individual school administrator who doesn’t know or won’t apply the rule. When you go back, bring everything you’ve gathered (UNHCR paper, any letter from an NGO, embassy letter) and say:

> *“I’ve been told by [UNHCR/StARS] that the Ministry allows temporary enrollment for Sudanese children who cannot provide their original birth certificate because of the war. I am requesting that temporary admission while I work on getting the original. If you still refuse, please give me a written refusal with the reason, so I can take it to the educational district office.”*

Asking for a written refusal often changes the dynamic — suddenly they become more willing to find a solution.

---

### 5. If the loop still isn’t broken, go one level up: the Educational Administration

Every area has a **local educational administration (الإدارة التعليمية)** that oversees schools. Find the one for your district and ask to speak to the **person responsible for refugee enrollment** or simply the director. Take all your papers and explain the deadlock. They have the authority to instruct the school to accept your son on an exceptional basis.

---

### Who you really need to talk to, in one sentence

The person who can break the cycle is **a protection or civil documentation officer at UNHCR Sixth of October, backed up if necessary by a legal aid lawyer from StARS or EFRR**. They have the power to issue a substitute document or force the school’s hand. The loop you’re stuck in exists because each office is treating your problem as someone else’s job. You fix that by not leaving any office without either a document that works, or a written referral that forces the next office to act.

You are already doing the hardest thing — showing up every day, carrying that paper, trying to build a future for your son. The system is broken, but you can make it work by becoming the person who refuses to be sent back to the first office without a concrete result. Take a deep breath, and start with UNHCR using the words above. You are your son’s best advocate, and there are people inside those offices who do want to help — they just need to be asked the right question.
